subChunks.title: ExecutorService & CompletableFuture

storyBeats.text: Eldrin replaces the golem-summoning ritual with a golem pool — four golems wait in the antechamber. Tasks are queued; idle golems grab work immediately.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Creating a new thread for every tiny task is like hiring a new wizard every time you need a single spell cast. A thread pool keeps workers ready and reuses them. The ExecutorService manages the pool; you simply submit tasks.

storyBeats.label: ExecutorService basics

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: CompletableFuture takes this further — you chain asynchronous steps like a pipeline, each triggered when the previous completes. The main thread is never blocked. It is the foundation of reactive and async Java code.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Use CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() to supply the string "Hello", chain thenApply to append " Apprentice", then print with join().

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between ExecutorService and CompletableFuture? When would you use each?

options: Blocks the calling thread until the result is available
questions.answer: Blocks the calling thread until the result is available
questions.explanation: get() is a blocking call — it waits until the async computation finishes and returns the result (or throws if it failed).

subChunks.title: Concurrent Collections & Atomic Variables

storyBeats.text: Eldrin points to the academy's chaotic message board — apprentices simultaneously posting and reading, messages appearing corrupted.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Standard collections were designed for single-threaded use. Put multiple threads in them without coordination and you get data corruption, lost updates, and ConcurrentModificationException. The concurrent package has purpose-built thread-safe versions.

storyBeats.label: ConcurrentHashMap

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: ConcurrentHashMap achieves thread safety without locking the entire map — it uses segment-level locking. Reads are almost always non-blocking. For most concurrent map needs, it is the right choice.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Use ConcurrentHashMap to count word frequencies. Start 3 threads, each adding "spell" five times using merge(). Print the final count for "spell".
guidedPractice.hint: freq.merge("spell", 1, Integer::sum) atomically increments the count. Join all threads before reading.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why is ConcurrentHashMap preferable to a synchronized HashMap? When would you use a BlockingQueue?

questions.prompt: You need a thread-safe counter that many threads increment and you occasionally check the value. The best option is:
questions.explanation: AtomicInteger provides atomic increment without locks — faster than synchronized for a single counter. volatile only ensures visibility, not atomicity of ++.
